claim: Above about $1M a year of COGS, get each factory to break every SKU into components, sub-vendors, labour, overhead, financing cost and factory margin.
body: Roman Khan, who buys and runs DTC brands, says 99 of 100 founders he meets in acquisitions have no bill of materials, while large apparel brands negotiate from one by default. His BOM columns: each component and its cost, the sub-supplier and source, lead time, country of origin, payment terms, plus separate lines for factory labour, factory overhead, credit insurance, financing cost and the factory's margin. For a gold and lab-grown diamond ring that means the diamond sub-vendor, gold bought at the intraday price when the PO is placed, setting and polishing labour (about $42 in his example), and so on. How he builds it: tell the factory you plan to grow volume several times over, physically take the product apart (zip, buttons, lining, fibre), test claims such as organic cotton, then design the BOM with the supplier; for a new factory, ask it to source sub-vendors and build its own BOM rather than sharing the old one. Benefits: visible margin inflation (an Indian textile supplier was running 25 to 35%, which he calls abnormal for textiles, and gave a concession), tariff impact by line, monthly quotes from 6 or 7 sub-vendors on opaque inputs, and product ideas such as 10K versus 14K gold. His threshold: about $1M a year in COGS (roughly $100k a month wired, as little as $2.5M revenue).
conditions: Brands with their own manufactured products (private label or custom) spending roughly $1M+ a year on COGS; factories that assemble from bought-in components.
fails_when: Very small buyers with no volume leverage, where factories refuse open-book costing; fully commoditised catalogue products; relationships where demanding labour costs damages goodwill without a growth story behind it.

claim: Negotiate price breaks per BOM line around how fully the factory uses labour dedicated to your line; such volume credits are worth $1 to $3 a unit.
body: Khan's method treats price breaks as a question about the factory's costs, not a haggle over the total. For each BOM line ask: at what volume does this input get cheaper (cotton, zips, labour)? The largest lever is fixed labour: if the factory has, say, 30 workers dedicated to your assembly line, filling that line closer to full utilisation each month lets it pass on $2 to $3 a unit. Sub-vendors also give volume breaks to the factory (he cites about $1 off a zip from a large zip maker), which you can ask to have passed through. These are structured as credits rather than up-front discounts: you hit the volume, then the lower price applies going forward. His head of production sits with the supplier to reconcile sub-vendor invoices, which makes the factory effectively an assembler and procurement arm. The next step he is taking is to buy major components (gold, diamonds) directly and supply the factory, removing the factory's markup on items where it carries inventory risk; he notes this also exposes you to commodity price swings (gold moved from about $2,000 to $5,000). Know competitor COGS for comparable products before the conversation; his volume ask comes with a credible plan to multiply orders.
conditions: Brands with a dedicated or semi-dedicated production line, open-book BOM, and a credible growth forecast; components with traceable market prices.
fails_when: Low or erratic volumes that cannot lift utilisation; factories with many small clients and no dedicated line; buying components directly without the working capital or commodity-risk appetite.

claim: Keep factories aware you have backup suppliers and share competing quotes; a sourcing agent argues hiding alternatives invites price and quality slippage.
body: The guest, who runs a sourcing agency serving seven-figure-plus ecommerce brands, says many brands fear that telling their factory or agent about other suppliers will damage the relationship; his view is the opposite. Mechanism: a supplier who believes it has no competition has room to raise prices or relax quality, while one that knows the brand has live alternatives must keep earning the business. How to apply: 1) Maintain at least one qualified backup factory per key SKU, with approved samples on file. 2) Request quotes from alternatives periodically, and show your main supplier the competing price (without naming the factory if that breaches confidentiality). 3) Use the comparison to negotiate unit price, payment terms or quality commitments rather than only switching. 4) Pair it with a documented production checklist; his agency runs an 80-step process per product because small misses (wrong colour, misplaced print) can ruin a run, and a 100,000 run produced wrong costs both the goods and the sales window. 5) Gate any switch on sample approval and a watch on returns after the first run. COVID supply breaks are his example of why brands now build contingencies. No price-reduction figures are given.
conditions: Brands manufacturing private-label or custom products overseas (China and Southeast Asia), with volumes large enough for factories to compete.
fails_when: Small buyers below a factory's priority threshold, where open shopping around may simply lose the slot; highly specialised suppliers with proprietary tooling or formulas where switching is impractical; cultures and relationships where long-term loyalty earns priority capacity in peak season.

claim: Moving production out of China is a lead-time versus cost trade: the guest's Egypt example adds about 30% to lead time while cutting cost basis about 30%.
body: The guest's agency moves production from China to Cambodia, Sri Lanka, Vietnam, Thailand, Egypt and Pakistan, and frames each move as a calculation, not a trend. Factors he weighs: where the raw material comes from (fabric often still comes from China, which adds transit), labour cost, taxes and duties, and where the country's manufacturing base is heading. His worked example: moving to Egypt might lengthen lead time by about 30% while lowering cost basis by about 30%, and in that case he generally favours cost. How to apply: 1) For each SKU, model landed cost (unit, freight, duty, tariffs for your import market) and total lead time per candidate country. 2) Translate the longer lead time into extra safety stock and cash tied up, since a 30% longer cycle means more inventory on order or on the water. 3) Compare the cost saving per unit times annual volume with the added carrying cost and stockout risk. 4) Prefer the move for stable, predictable best-sellers; keep fast-changing or trend SKUs close to the material source. 5) Run a sample and a small first order before shifting volume. He also notes small-scale hubs (Bali) are good for testing fabrics and short runs but expensive and slow to scale.
conditions: Brands with steady volume on core SKUs and enough cash to carry longer lead times; tariff exposure on Chinese imports (e.g. US).
fails_when: Cash-tight brands that cannot fund extra inventory in transit; trend-driven or seasonal products where a 30% longer lead time misses the selling window; categories where the new country lacks raw materials or skilled factories.

claim: Write tech packs in exact measurements (e.g. 4 inches from top, 2 from each side), never words like 'centred', and send factories a physical reference sample to copy.
body: The guest's quality rule is not to let the factory make any decision for you. Words that feel precise to a brand, such as 'centred', 'small logo' or 'matte', are interpreted differently on the factory floor: centred vertically or horizontally, measured from the seam or the edge. Every open choice is a place for a costly error. How to apply: 1) Build a specification sheet or tech pack for each SKU that states every dimension as a measurement with a tolerance: print position from top and from each side, print size, stitch counts, colours by Pantone code, materials by weight and composition, packaging and labelling. 2) Include annotated photos or drawings for placements. 3) When a client or you already own a product with the right quality but too high a price, ship that physical item to the factory as a reference sample to replicate, rather than describing it. 4) Always get a sample from a new factory before committing, and compare it against the spec sheet line by line. 5) Keep the approved sample as the golden sample for future inspections. These steps sit inside his agency's 80-step sourcing checklist; no defect-rate figures are given.
conditions: Brands producing custom or private-label goods with a factory, especially apparel, accessories and printed merchandise.
fails_when: Stock products bought off the shelf with no customisation, where a tech pack adds little; very small first orders where the factory will not follow detailed specs without a minimum.

claim: Book a roughly $200 third-party inspection before the container leaves the factory, and pay the final balance only after it passes; at sea, faults cannot be fixed.
body: Defects found in your warehouse are expensive: the stock is paid for, freight is spent, and the factory has little reason to fix it. Fogarty's rule is a final random inspection at the factory before shipment, costing about $200, which he says can save $20,000 in damaged or inconsistent stock. The inspector pulls random units, checks measurements against the tech pack and the pre-production sample, verifies packaging, labelling and carton weights, and photographs everything. Small inconsistencies are flagged because they multiply at volume. If the report shows problems, the factory reworks before loading; you approve or reject the shipment on that report. The lever that makes this work is payment timing: structure terms so the final balance is paid only after the inspection passes, otherwise the factory has no incentive to correct anything. Treat it as insurance on every bulk order, not only the first one, since quality often drifts on reorders once a factory knows you.
conditions: Any bulk order from an overseas factory where the balance payment can be tied to an inspection result.
fails_when: The brand has already paid 100% upfront, so the inspection can document problems but not force a fix; or the order is so small that inspection cost is a large share of order value.

claim: Never send a factory a product without a tech pack, and approve in three sample stages (strike-off, pre-production, production); keep one golden sample yourself and one at the factory.
body: Fogarty's first big calming-blanket order arrived in three different shades of grey and different weights under one SKU, because the factory had no spec sheet and made its own assumptions. A factory optimises for throughput, so anything left undefined gets the cheapest or easiest choice. A tech pack closes those gaps: drawings or photos from every angle, exact materials and finishes (fabric GSM, trims, hardware), measurements for every size and variant, colourways with Pantone codes, labels, packaging and folding, care instructions, and a product name, version and date. A freelance product designer can build one for about $200. Then sample in stages. First a strike-off or small test for materials and prints. Then a pre-production sample that must match the tech pack exactly; for apparel, order several to confirm size grading. This becomes the gold standard: keep one in-house and leave one at the factory as the shared reference. Finally a production sample made just before bulk; if it does not match the pre-production standard, do not proceed. Get samples from several shortlisted suppliers (message 10 to 15 verified factories to start) and judge who follows instructions and updates without being chased, not only who makes the nicest piece.
conditions: Brands manufacturing their own or customised products with overseas factories, especially soft goods and apparel.
fails_when: The product is a stock catalogue item bought unchanged, where a full tech pack adds little; or the brand lacks the volume to get factories to work to a custom spec at all.

claim: Plan reorders on total lead time: production 20-30 days plus sea 30-40 days door to door (air 7-10); launch with an air batch, restock by sea.
body: Fogarty's working lead times: production often 20 to 30 days, sea freight 30 to 40 days door to door, air freight 7 to 10 days. So a sea restock takes roughly two months from purchase order to shelf, and a brand that reorders when it is nearly out of stock is already late. His habits: start planning the next shipment the day the current one lands; use a hybrid of a small air batch to start selling quickly and sea freight for the bulk restock, because air is fast but expensive; for large or heavy items, sea is almost always the answer. Feed these lead times into a reorder point (daily sales velocity times total lead time, plus safety stock): at 50 units a day, 60 days of lead time and 500 safety units, reorder at 3,500 units. Review velocity and stock weekly and share forecasts with suppliers and the freight forwarder. The cost of skipping this: when demand spiked to $200,000 days early in COVID, The Oodie sold out within a week and could not fulfil for almost two months; he estimates a dedicated planner would have made the company 30 to 40% bigger.
conditions: Brands importing stock by sea from Asia; lead times vary by route, product and season.
fails_when: Production is domestic or made-to-order, or freight markets are disrupted (port congestion, rate spikes), where the typical ranges understate lead time; air is uneconomic for heavy or bulky goods even at launch.

claim: Expect defects in bulk Chinese orders (300 of 10,000 here): order about 10% extra or pay for inspection, and test any cheaper new supplier with about 500 units first.
body: The poster's 10,000-unit order arrived with about 300 broken or poor-quality pieces, roughly 3%; returning them to the supplier was not worth the time and freight. Alibaba does not inspect goods for you, so the buyer owns quality. Rules drawn from it: 1) Budget an overage of about 10% of needed units, or hire a third-party pre-shipment inspection (the header cites about 200 per inspection), and inspect on arrival before shipping to customers. 2) Never move all volume to a new supplier on price. When a supplier offered the same item for about 20% less, the poster ordered 500 units as a test and most were defective, so the original supplier stayed. 3) Keep at least two qualified suppliers until the new one passes inspection on a real batch. 4) Get the supplier's email and WhatsApp or WeChat, because suppliers go silent on platform chat without notice. 5) Payment: the poster insists on Alibaba's payment gateway (Trade Assurance) over PayPal or direct transfer; a US sourcing agent in the comments disagrees, saying disputes often fail and he prefers bank transfer with a negotiated discount for the fee saved.

fails_when: Factories with strong QC and an agreed defect allowance in the contract, where 10% overage wastes cash; products where defects are safety-critical, where overage is no substitute for inspection.

claim: Moving from small AliExpress buys to Alibaba bulk cut one jewellery item from 7.80 to about 4.00 per unit, and to 2.00 at 10,000 units.
body: A US jewellery store buying about 500 units a week from AliExpress at 7.80 each (selling at 25.99) posted requests for quotation on Alibaba ahead of Q4. Quotes for the same item ranged from about 4.00 to 10.00, and the price at a 10,000-unit order was about 2.00. Separate negotiation on another order took the unit price from 6.00 to 4.80, saving about 3,500 per order. Takeaways: 1) Retail-style marketplaces price for small buyers; once a SKU is proven, RFQs to manufacturers can more than halve unit cost. 2) Quotes for an identical item vary widely, so collect several. 3) Ask for tiered prices at, for example, 1,000, 5,000 and 10,000 units and set the order size against cash and sell-through, not the lowest unit price alone. 4) Negotiate even after quoting; a 20% cut is realistic in this example. 5) Ask long-standing suppliers to upgrade shipping on large orders: this supplier moved from 10 to 14-day ePacket to 4 to 5-day FedEx to California at no extra charge. Plan heavy items early: a 1.2 kg steel product cost about 2,000 by air versus a month by sea container.

fails_when: Unproven products, where a 10,000-unit order risks dead stock; cash-tight brands for which the bigger order starves ad spend; the post is from before recent US tariff changes on Chinese goods, which alter landed cost.

claim: A tech pack with drawings, fabric spec (GSM and treatments), measurements, graphics, hardware and labels removes about 90% of supplier errors and lets you prove spec cutting by weighing fabric.
body: Fogarty learned this on weighted blankets: ordering 'a thousand weighted blankets in grey' from Alibaba produced a container where some boxes matched the sample and others did not. His fix is a technical pack for every product, with six parts: complete drawings (including exact print placement), fabric specification (weight in GSM and any treatments such as acid washing), full measurements for every size and grade, graphics files, hardware (zips, pockets, trims) and labels and packaging, plus reference photos of approved samples. In his experience this removes about 90% of supplier errors. It also gives you evidence: if a factory quietly reduces fabric weight, weighing pieces against the GSM in the tech pack proves it, and it makes moving to a new manufacturer far easier because the spec belongs to you. Add a third-party QC inspection (an inspection agent or firms such as SGS) for at least the first few production runs, and build a critical path listing every step from fabric strike-off and first sample to inspection and PO, with a duration on each step.

claim: Find personal-care manufacturers by learning who makes for leading brands, then vet capacity and certifications; Salt & Stone now splits volume across about 10 contract manufacturers.
body: Salt & Stone's founder (the brand reports $165M+ revenue) says personal-care contract manufacturing is harder to find than overseas factories for hard goods. His method: identify which factories produce for the category leaders, by reaching people who work or worked at those brands on LinkedIn and asking for a few minutes, or paying them as a short-term consultant for manufacturer names. He did the same earlier for sunglasses, tracing where a major eyewear brand produced. His most expensive production mistake was trusting a contract manufacturer without full vetting. Big brands have budgets to audit factories for capacity, quality and certifications, so a manufacturer's existing client list is a useful vetting signal; small brands in a hurry to launch skip this. On formula copying: manufacturers do make variants of successful formulas for others, and brands copied his stick mould, colours and scent names, yet he says the copies sell a tenth as much, so the defence is brand plus product, not secrecy. At deodorant volume he uses about 10 manufacturers rather than one.

claim: With a sole-source supplier, secure change-of-control continued supply plus most-favoured-nation clauses on price and on inventory (first right to any open capacity).
body: Peter Rahal's RXBAR nearly failed mid-growth when a larger customer bought out the contract manufacturer's volume and RXBAR could not get product made; switching manufacturers mid-scale carried its own risks. At David Protein, the key ingredient (an EPG fat replacer) came from one supplier, so before acquiring that supplier he had negotiated a supply agreement with three protections. First, continued supply on change of control: if the supplier is sold, the new owner must keep supplying. Second, most-favoured-nation pricing: if any other buyer gets a better price, yours is matched. Third, most-favoured-nation inventory: you get first right to any open supply or capacity. He later acquired the supplier outright to remove the dependency and secure the ingredient's other uses. How to apply: list every input with a single qualified source (ingredient, co-manufacturer, packaging), and for each, negotiate change-of-control, MFN price and MFN capacity clauses in the supply agreement before you scale volume through them, while starting qualification of a second source. Acquisition is the extreme option when the input is also your product moat.
conditions: Brands with a critical ingredient, formula or manufacturing step available from one supplier; CPG and food especially.
fails_when: Small brands with no negotiating leverage, where a supplier will not grant MFN terms; commoditised inputs with many suppliers, where dual sourcing is cheaper than contract protections.

claim: In India, IGST on imported goods is charged on assessable value plus customs duties; a GST-registered importer can claim the IGST back as input tax credit, but never the basic customs duty.
body: The government flyer on imports under GST says all imports are treated as inter-State supplies, so integrated tax (IGST) is charged in addition to basic customs duty, collected at the point customs duty is levied. The value for IGST is the assessable value plus the customs duty and any other duty charged in the same manner as customs duty; its worked example takes an assessable value of Rs 100, adds 10% basic duty and a cess to reach Rs 110.30, and charges IGST on that. Input tax credit of the IGST and compensation cess paid at import is available to the importer, so IGST is in essence a pass-through for a registered business. Basic customs duty (and the education cess in the example) is not available as input tax credit. The importer declares its GSTIN. For a landed cost sheet this means: basic customs duty and any surcharge on it are a real cost per unit; IGST is a cash outlay that comes back as credit for a GST-registered store, but is a real cost for a store that cannot claim credit.
conditions: Goods imported into India by a business; rates in the example are illustrative and the duty rate for each product comes from the current Customs Tariff by HSN code.
fails_when: The importer is not GST-registered or cannot use the credit (for example under the composition scheme), in which case IGST is a cost; duty rates and surcharges change by notification, so the flyer's example rates are not current rates.
numbers: Worked example: assessable value Rs 100, basic customs duty 10%, value for IGST Rs 110.30

claim: US duty is charged on the price paid to the seller excluding international freight and insurance, plus packing costs, selling commissions, assists such as moulds you supply, and royalties.
body: CBP's guide to customs value says the transaction value is the price actually paid or payable when sold for export to the US, which excludes international freight, insurance and other C.I.F. charges, plus amounts for packing costs incurred by the buyer, selling commissions incurred by the buyer, the apportioned value of any assist (for example moulds, tools or artwork the buyer gives the factory), and royalties or licence fees paid as a condition of sale. For a landed cost sheet this means duty is calculated on the factory price (adjusted for those additions), not on the freight-inclusive cost, and a mould paid for separately still has to be spread over units and declared. Proof of the actual freight cost should come from the carrier's documents.
conditions: Commercial imports into the US valued by transaction value, the primary method.
fails_when: Related-party sales, or freight that cannot be documented, where CBP may value differently; other countries such as India value goods differently, so the rule does not carry across.

claim: A US textile label needs fibre content by percentage, the country of origin on the front of the label, and the maker's name or RN number; at a neck, the origin label sits inside centre of the neck.
body: The FTC's guide to the Textile and Wool Acts says each generic fibre must be listed with its percentage by weight in descending order, in English, with fibres under 5% usually grouped as other fibre. The country of origin names the country where the product was made and must be on the front of the label; for garments with a neck it goes inside centre of the neck, between the shoulder seams or next to another neck label, and no other label may hide it. The manufacturer or dealer is identified by full business name or a Registered Identification Number with its RN prefix. Labels must stay attached until the product reaches the buyer, and required terms are not abbreviated. For a factory spec sheet, the label artwork, its wording and its exact sewn position belong in the spec, not left to the factory.
conditions: Textile and wool products sold in the US.
fails_when: Products outside the Acts' scope, or other categories with their own rules (children's products, cosmetics, electronics).

claim: In India, a pre-packaged product must declare maker, packer or importer, country of origin for imports, generic name, net quantity, month and year of manufacture, MRP inclusive of all taxes, unit sale price and consumer care details.

For a factory spec sheet, these lines must be on the retail pack artwork before printing, with the Indian importer's details, not the factory's, where goods are imported.

claim: Many product launches sell their first 30 to 40% of stock to the email list and existing fans, then stall in grade C or D, so retire SKUs as you add them or launches keep locking cash in stock.
body: Launches are one of the strongest growth levers, but single-product giants can mislead. Supplement brands such as AG1 can reposition one product for many needs (gut, hair, energy) and reach a huge market without new SKUs. Most categories cannot, so they need new products to grow, and many launches fail. The usual pattern: a launch pops with organic followers and existing customers, sells the first 30 to 40%, then barely moves. Each one adds stock to the balance sheet and limits the cash available for scaling. claim: Small brands are usually limited by the cash cycle, not ads: with a 90-day lead time and full payment upfront you can sit 90 days out of stock; a 20% deposit, a 30-day supplier or inventory finance shrinks that gap.
body: When the gross profit from one order is the only funding for the next, each purchase order can be only slightly bigger than the last: sell 10 units, earn enough to buy 11, then 12. Add a 90-day production lead time and full payment upfront, which small orders often require, and you cannot reorder until the current stock has sold, so you sit out of stock for about 90 days. Three fixes. Negotiate deposit terms, for example 20% upfront and the balance on shipment, so the next order goes in after selling a fraction of current stock; in Blue Sense's example that cuts the out-of-stock gap to roughly the 20-day shipping time. Find a manufacturer with a shorter lead time, such as 30 days instead of 90. Or use inventory finance, repaying from sales and rolling into the next order. Finance is expensive, usually needs you to put yourself up as security, and only works if the stock sells at the planned efficiency. How to apply: map your cash conversion cycle (days of inventory plus days of receivables minus days of payables) and attack the biggest part first.

claim: Allbirds shows the overstock trap: revenue rose about 30% while inventory doubled, then came a $19.1M write-down and gross margin fell from 52% to 43%.
body: Allbirds' public filings make a clear case of stock growing faster than sales. Net revenue went from about $220 million to $277 million to $297 million over three years, while inventory roughly doubled. The filings attribute a $48.5 million inventory increase to more stock in transit from longer lead times and higher inbound freight. Cash on hand fell year after year as money moved into stock. The next year the company booked a $19.1 million loss tied to writing down and liquidating first-generation apparel, and gross margin dropped from 52% to 43%, also hit by freight, warehousing, more promotions (likely to raise cash) and unfavourable exchange rates. Blue Sense reads it as C and D grade stock building up until it had to be cleared. How to apply: each quarter compare inventory growth with revenue growth. If inventory is growing much faster, find which SKUs drove it, check whether longer lead times are the cause, and cut future buys before you are forced into discounting. Treat rising promotions as a possible sign of a cash squeeze, not only a marketing choice.

claim: Paying a supplier 2% more to move from net 30 to net 60 is a one-month loan costing about 24% a year, dearer than a typical bank loan at 15 to 16%.
body: Longer supplier terms feel like free cash and a 2% price bump sounds small, so many brands accept the trade. Convert it to an annual rate first. The extra 30 days is a one-month loan of the full order value (you owe the whole amount for the whole month, so the average balance is 100%), and the 2% fee buys one twelfth of a year. That works out to roughly 24% a year; Blue Sense's slide showed 24.3%. This is why suppliers agree so readily: they earn close to a 24% annual return on the cash they float you. Compare that with a bank loan quoted at about 15 to 16% APR, which in Blue Sense's comparison was the cheapest money available, even though it looked the least exciting, because banks quote the annual rate plainly. How to apply: before agreeing to longer terms in exchange for a higher unit cost, calculate fee divided by (average balance times years) for the extension and compare it with your cheapest facility. If a bank line or overdraft costs less, borrow from the bank and keep the lower unit price. Longer terms still make sense when you cannot get bank credit, or when the cash funds stock that sells quickly at a high margin.

claim: Plan buys with open-to-buy: planned sales at cost plus planned end-of-month stock, minus beginning stock, minus stock on order; it breaks when the forecast misses, orders arrive late or stock counts are wrong.
body: Open-to-buy (OTB) answers how much inventory to order for a future month. Take planned sales for that month at cost (for example $760,000 of cost of goods for October, not revenue), add the stock you want left at month end, subtract stock you will start the month with, and subtract anything already on order or in transit. What remains is what you can buy. It replaces the habit of rough guesses from when the brand was small. Blue Sense flags three ways it goes wrong. 1. Revenue misses the forecast, especially when you plan fast growth, so you end up overstocked and short of cash. 2. Inbound orders are delayed, so you are understocked even though the numbers looked right. 3. The inputs are wrong, for example beginning stock in the system does not match what is really on hand. How to apply: build OTB by month and by category, feed it from your sales plan, review it weekly against actual sales, and re-cut future orders when sales run below plan. Reconcile stock counts before each buy.

Add a 90-day lead time and full payment upfront because orders are small, and you must sell out before you can reorder, then wait 90 days out of stock. How to apply: map your current cycle in days, then negotiate terms and lead times before borrowing, and model interest cost against the extra contribution the stock will produce.

claim: Under DDP the foreign seller must clear import and pay your country's duties and taxes, which some countries do not let foreign firms do; ICC suggests DAP, where the buyer clears import, instead.
body: DDP quotes from Chinese suppliers and their forwarders are tempting because the price looks all-in. But DDP makes the seller responsible for import formalities in your country, at its own cost and risk. Some countries bar a foreign company from acting as the importer, so the seller or its forwarder may use a third party as importer, declare a value you never see, or recover the duty in the unit price with a margin on top. You also lose control of the customs entry that your business is answerable for. How to apply it: if a supplier offers DDP, ask who will be the importer of record, what value will be declared, and whether you will receive the entry documents. For regular stock orders, prefer DAP or FCA and use your own customs broker, so the duty, the import VAT or GST and the entry are in your name and on your books. Keep DDP for small trial orders where speed matters more than cost control, and check the landed cost against a DAP quote plus your broker's fee.

fails_when: The seller is properly registered as an importer in your country, or a tiny trial order where the convenience is worth more than the control.

claim: Avoid EXW when goods cross a border: the buyer must load the truck at its own risk and handle export clearance, so ICC tells traders to use FCA instead.
body: An EXW price looks cheapest because it stops at the factory gate. But under EXW the buyer pays for and bears the risk of loading at the factory, arranges all transport and must clear the goods for export. In China, export declarations are normally filed by the exporter of record, so a foreign buyer on EXW depends on the factory or a forwarder's paperwork anyway, and any damage during loading is the buyer's loss. FCA moves export clearance and loading onto the seller while still letting you choose and pay your own forwarder. How to apply it: when a factory quotes EXW, ask it to requote FCA at its own premises. The gap between the two prices is the true cost of loading and export clearance; compare it with what your forwarder would charge for the same origin work. Never compare an EXW price with another factory's FOB or FCA price without adding those origin costs first, or the EXW supplier will look cheaper than it is.

claim: For goods shipped in containers, buy on FCA (named terminal or factory) rather than FOB; ICC reserves FOB for bulk cargo loaded port to port onto a ship.
body: FOB was written before containers existed. Under FOB the seller carries the risk until the goods are on board the vessel, but a container is handed over at a terminal and can sit there for days before loading. FCA matches what really happens: risk passes when the seller hands the goods to the carrier you named, either loaded onto your collecting truck at the factory or ready to unload at the terminal. How to apply it: in your RFQ ask for prices on 'FCA [factory address]' or 'FCA [terminal, port]' as well as FOB, and name the port, for example FCA Yantian terminal. Ask the factory what charges it includes up to that point (export clearance, terminal handling). Then let your own forwarder quote from that point. If a factory only understands FOB, accept FOB, but write the named port and confirm in the PO that export clearance and loading costs sit with the seller. Many forwarders still book container freight on FOB by habit, so the switch matters most when goods wait at a terminal or when you pay by letter of credit, where Incoterms 2020 lets the buyer tell its carrier to issue an on-board bill of lading to the seller under FCA.

body: Fair Wear's product costing sheet is a clean template for any cut and sew should-cost, and it shows where a factory hides money. Step 1: list every BOM line with its cost per garment: fabric (consumption per piece times price per metre or kilo), accessories and trims, then polybag, packaging and labels as their own lines. In the polo shirt example, materials come to $1.35 a piece. Step 2: add the CM cost (cut and make): working minute cost times the sewing minutes the style needs. Step 3: add factory overhead, outsourced processes such as printing or embroidery ($0.20 in the example), inbound and outbound logistics, and any import duties the factory pays on fabric. That sum is total cost, about $1.75 in the example. Step 4: add the factory's profit margin (10% here) and, if an agent or buying house sits in the middle, its commission (3% here). The result is the FOB price, about $1.98. How to use it: ask the factory to fill these same rows, then compare each row with your own estimate. A gap in materials means check consumption and fabric price; a gap in CM means check minutes and efficiency; a gap at the bottom means margin or a hidden agent. claim: Check a wage-rise price increase by the labour minute: in Fair Wear's polo, moving to a higher target wage lifts labour from $0.20 to $0.54 a piece but FOB only 19.6%, and a minimum wage step only 5.3%.
body: When a factory asks for more because a minimum wage rose, the fair increase is the change in labour cost per piece plus the factory's margin and commission on top, not a flat percentage of the whole price. Fair Wear's calculator isolates labour for exactly this. The factory works out a labour minute value (total monthly labour cost per worker divided by monthly working minutes), then divides it by the direct labour share of its wage bill to get a factory labour minute value. Their example: BDT 1.1026 per minute divided by a 60% direct share gives BDT 1.8376. Add overhead per minute for the working minute cost, then multiply by actual sewing minutes. In the polo example, labour per piece is $0.199 at one minimum wage, $0.291 at the next and $0.542 at a target wage, which moves FOB up 5.3% and 19.6%. How to apply it: ask for the old and new labour minute value and the minutes per style, recompute labour per piece, then add the same profit and commission rates. Agree to that amount. If the ask is far above it, the gap is margin, not wages.

claim: Cut and make cost = working minute cost x SAM / line efficiency; an 18 minute polo sewn at 60% efficiency takes 30 real minutes, so efficiency moves labour cost as much as wages do.
body: This is the standard formula garment factories use, so learn its terms before you negotiate CM. SMV (standard minute value) is the time a trained operator needs for each operation. SAM (standard allowed minutes) is SMV plus allowances for bundles, machines and personal time. Line efficiency is SAM divided by the minutes the line really uses. The working minute cost is the factory's labour cost per minute (including indirect staff) plus overhead per minute. CM per garment = working minute cost x SAM / efficiency. In Fair Wear's polo example, SAM is 18 minutes at 60% efficiency, which means 30 actual sewing minutes. Their trouser example: SAM 35 minutes, but the line needed 56.5, which is 61.9% efficiency. How to apply it: ask the factory for SAM per style (ideally from a time system such as GSD) and the efficiency they assumed. Check the efficiency against your order: Fair Wear notes it depends on the line, the order quantity and the number of colours and sizes. Then you can test any CM quote in minutes, not just dollars.
conditions: Sewn products (apparel, bags, soft goods) from factories that cost by minutes.
fails_when: Factories that quote a lump CM figure and refuse to share minutes, or highly automated products where machine time, not sewing labour, drives cost.

claim: Put a fixed liquidated damages figure in China contracts, such as a daily rate for late delivery; China has no 30% cap, and courts treat damages more than 30% above the actual loss as possibly excessive.
body: Factories rarely take a promise to cover 'all losses' seriously, because lost sales are hard to prove. A fixed figure, called 违约金 in Chinese, deters breach and gives you a starting number. Use a daily rate where the harm grows over time, such as late delivery or tooling held back; the law firm's example is RMB 20,000 per day, so 18 days late gives RMB 360,000. Use a fixed sum for breaches that are hard to prove, such as RMB 500,000 per unauthorised production run. Match the figure to the harm: a sum suited to a large company's core technology looks absurd on a first RMB 300,000 order. Myth to drop: Chinese law does not cap damages at 30%. Under the Supreme People's Court's 2023 interpretation, damages more than 30% above the actual loss caused by the breach may be seen as too high, but the benchmark is the loss, not the order value, and courts can also raise a figure that is too low. Write down how you chose the number. Chinese courts can freeze a factory's bank accounts before judgment up to the claim amount, generally deciding within five days, or 48 hours if urgent.

fails_when: Contracts enforced outside China under laws that treat penalty clauses differently, or a figure with no link to any plausible loss.

claim: Pay only the Chinese company that signed your contract, into its approved company account; payments to Hong Kong, personal, broker or related-company accounts create fraud risk and weaken enforcement.
body: A China law firm's view is that payment terms shape factory behaviour as much as the contract does. When a factory has more orders than capacity it serves first the customers whose money is still to come, so a buyer who has paid in full is the easiest to delay. Two rules follow. First, keep a holdback until after inspection or delivery, tied to events anyone can verify, such as a passed inspection report or the arrival date. Second, pay only the Chinese company that is party to your contract, into an account confirmed in writing before any money moves. A wire to a Hong Kong trading arm, a salesperson's personal account or a 'related company' makes it hard to prove who you paid, and is the most common route for invoice fraud when bank details 'change' by email or WeChat. How to apply it: confirm bank details by phone with a known contact before the first payment and whenever they change. Also write clear quality standards and notice deadlines, because if you withhold payment on weak terms the factory may file a claim with Sinosure, China's export credit insurer.

body: Buyers often sign an NNN and assume they are covered. It protects information and relationships, but says nothing about what the factory must deliver. A manufacturing agreement fills that gap. Its core terms: quality standards that can be measured, referring to the spec sheet and a physical golden sample kept by the buyer, not words like 'good quality'; inspection rights, the acceptance procedure and who decides whether goods pass; delivery dates and the remedy if they slip; what happens to goods that fail; tooling ownership, location, use, maintenance and return, with a ban on the factory pledging, moving, scrapping or lending it; and a ban on moving production to another plant without written approval, since many quality and tooling problems start when work quietly moves. It should also cover price, quantities, payment, IP and disputes, and be enforceable in China, usually in Chinese under Chinese law. A factory can keep your drawings secret and still use them to make the product for itself or a rival, build a near copy, pass work to an affiliate, or sell directly to your customers once it learns who they are. An NNN agreement covers all three: non-use limits your information to the work you authorise; non-disclosure controls who may receive it, such as mould makers and component suppliers, and who is responsible if they misuse it; non-circumvention bars the factory from using customers, suppliers or deals it learned through you. Adding 'non-use' words to a translated NDA is not a reliable fix. How to apply it: sign before the factory sees any drawings, samples or prices. claim: In a bilingual China contract the Chinese text usually controls in Chinese courts, even when the English says otherwise, so have every key term and number back-translated by someone not working for the factory.
body: If both versions name Chinese as controlling, or if they conflict, the Chinese version governs in Chinese courts and arbitration. In one case the English required a part to withstand 500 pounds of pressure and the Chinese said 300; the 300 applies. In another, the English barred a distributor from selling competing goods and the Chinese allowed it. So the document that matters is the one many buyers cannot read. How to apply it: draft in Chinese with a good English translation, and have the Chinese checked by your own lawyer or translator, never by the factory. Make a habit of back-translation for everything that sets money or quality: ask a second person to translate the Chinese PO or spec back into English without seeing your original, then compare. Learn the words you will meet on every quote: 起订量 (MOQ), 打样 and 打样费 (sampling, sample fee), 大货 (bulk production), 交期 (lead time or delivery date), 出厂价 (ex-factory price), 含税 and 不含税 (tax included or excluded), 定金 and 尾款 (deposit and balance), 模具费 (mould fee), 验货 (inspection) and 违约金 (liquidated damages). A China law firm's checklist: define tooling broadly (moulds, dies, jigs, fixtures, gauges, prototypes, CAD files and drawings); state when ownership passes to you and that the factory holds the tools only as custodian; attach a schedule listing each tool with photos, ID number and current location; require permanent plates marking them as your property; require written approval before any tool moves; get current editable design files and neutral formats such as STEP or IGES during the relationship; set a firm release deadline, delivery place, packing and export papers, with real consequences such as daily liquidated damages. Ask early who actually makes the mould; the factory may subcontract it to a mould shop you never meet. For expensive tools, consider contracting with the mould shop directly. Do not announce a move until you know where every tool is.

claim: Gross up each BOM line for expected scrap: required quantity times (1 + scrap rate), so 100 pieces at 10% component scrap means buying and costing 110.
body: A BOM that lists only the quantity that ends up in the finished product understates both purchase quantity and unit cost. ERP systems such as SAP handle this with a component scrap percentage on each BOM line: the system multiplies the needed quantity by one plus the scrap rate, then costs and orders the larger number. SAP's own example: 100 pieces of a raw material with 10% component scrap are costed and planned as 110, with 10 counted as scrap. How to apply it in a spreadsheet BOM: add a scrap % column per line (fabric cutting loss, resin purge and rejects, broken inserts, misprinted labels), compute gross quantity = net quantity x (1 + scrap %), and multiply gross quantity by price to get the line cost. Then divide total cost by the good units only. Ask the factory for its own loss allowances per line; they already use them in their quote. Note the method: SAP adds scrap on top of the net quantity. A yield-based method divides by yield instead (100 / 0.9 = 111.1), which gives slightly more. Pick one method and use it on every line, or your should-cost and the factory's will never match. A BOM-level scrap value overrides any default set on the material itself, so set scrap where the loss really happens.

fails_when: Bought-in finished goods with no processing loss, or lines where the factory carries the scrap at its own cost under a fixed price.

claim: Scrap compounds across BOM levels: 10% assembly scrap then 10% component scrap on 200 units needs 242 components, not 240, because each rate applies to the already grossed-up quantity.
body: In a multi-level BOM (finished SKU, then sub-assemblies, then parts and raw material), losses at each level stack. SAP calculates assembly scrap first and then component scrap, and adds the scrap from both. With 10% at each level, 200 finished units become 220 at the assembly level and 242 at the component level, so 42 parts are scrap, not the 40 you get by adding the two rates. Over three or four levels, or with higher losses such as 15% fabric cutting loss on top of 5% sewing rejects, the gap grows. How to apply it: work from the top of the BOM down. Start with good finished units, divide or multiply by each level's loss in turn, and only then multiply the bottom-level quantity by its price. Do it per level in separate columns so you can see which level's loss drives cost. When a factory's material quantity looks high, rebuild it this way before arguing; often the factory is right and your BOM simply skipped a level. When it is still high after compounding, ask which loss rate they use at each step and compare it with your inspection data.
conditions: Products with two or more processing stages that each lose material, such as fabric then garment, or moulded part then assembly.
fails_when: Single-stage products, or where later stages only fit parts after defective units are already removed (then the earlier loss should not carry through).

claim: Do not load assembly scrap onto parts fitted after faulty units are pulled out: in SAP's example, 1,000 bikes at 10% assembly scrap need 1,100 of an early part but only 1,010 of a late part.
body: A common BOM mistake is to apply the same loss rate to every component. That overstates the cost of parts that go in late. In SAP's example, a factory needs 1,000 finished bicycles and expects 10% assembly scrap. A component fitted early carries that loss, so 1,100 are needed. A component fitted after the faulty assemblies have already been removed only carries its own 1% operation loss, so 1,010 are needed. SAP models this with a 'net' flag on the BOM line that switches off assembly scrap for that part. How to apply it to a consumer product: map the process in order (for example mould, assemble, test, then fit the battery, then pack). Ask the factory where units are tested and rejected. Parts and packaging added after the last reject point should carry only their own handling loss. This matters most for expensive late parts such as batteries, electronics, gift boxes and printed sleeves. If a factory quotes the same 8% or 10% loss on your retail box as on the moulded body, ask to move the box after the test step in the costing.

fails_when: Products where every part is fitted before any check, or where late steps themselves damage earlier parts.

claim: Carton drop tests follow ISTA 1A heights by packed weight: 760 mm up to 10 kg, 610 mm to 19 kg, 460 mm to 28 kg, 310 mm to 45 kg and 200 mm to 68 kg.
body: Transit damage shows up as returns and one-star reviews, and it is cheap to screen at the factory. ISTA 1A sets the drop height from the packed weight: 0 to 10 kg (to 21 lb) 760 mm or 30 in; 10 to 19 kg 610 mm or 24 in; 19 to 28 kg 460 mm or 18 in; 28 to 45 kg 310 mm or 12 in; 45 to 68 kg 200 mm or 8 in. The drops start on the most fragile corner, then the three edges from that corner, shortest to longest, then the six faces, for 10 drops in the standard sequence. ISTA 1A also has a fixed-displacement vibration test at 25 mm (1 inch) peak to peak. Before testing, decide what counts as a fail: product damage, which damage is tolerable, and what state the pack must be in afterwards. Dented carton corners alone are normally not a fail. How to apply: ask the inspector to drop one or two export cartons per inspection (a special-level sample) and open them to check the product. For parcel shipping to consumers, ask a lab for the ISTA 3 series, which simulates parcel networks such as FedEx or UPS, because a single unit in a mailer takes harder knocks than a full export carton.

claim: MIL-STD-105, ANSI Z1.4 and ISO 2859-1 share the same basic sampling tables, so a PO can cite any one and inspectors anywhere will draw the same sample.
body: The US military issued MIL-STD-105D in 1963; ANSI adopted it as Z1.4 in 1971 and ISO adopted it with minor changes as ISO 2859 in 1974. The last military revision, 105E, came in 1989, and the basic tables stayed the same throughout. That is why QIMA, V-Trust, Bureau Veritas and most Asian inspection firms quote 'ANSI/ASQ Z1.4' or 'ISO 2859-1' interchangeably. NIST also stresses that the scheme is meant to start with normal inspection and follow the switching rules, tightening when evidence shows the producer is missing the agreed AQL. How to apply: in the PO and quality agreement write one line such as 'Sampling to ISO 2859-1 (equivalent ANSI/ASQ Z1.4), single sampling, normal inspection, general level II, AQL 0 / 2.5 / 4.0 for critical / major / minor, switching rules apply.' This removes any later argument that a different table was used. If a factory proposes its own in-house AQL table, ask which standard it follows and compare a few rows before you accept it.

claim: Squeezing price without locking the spec invites 'quality fade', quiet material cuts across runs; one case found an aluminium part under 90% of its specified weight.
body: Paul Midler named the pattern in 2007: each production run carries a little less of the required input than the approved sample, a sub-supplier swaps a cheaper component, or a spec is reduced without telling the buyer. His cases include an aluminium part for building systems that weighed under 90% of its specified weight, cartons that began collapsing after more than a year of imports, and a soap supplier that tested 10 samples, saw 9 fail and sent only the passing result. The drivers are hard price pressure, payment before shipment and little reputational cost to the factory. How to apply it: before you push on price, write down every point you will check on every shipment, such as product weight, wall thickness, material certificate, fabric GSM and carton strength, and keep a signed golden sample. Weigh and measure a few units from each batch against the first approved batch and track the numbers. Own your design files, bill of materials and moulds so you can walk away. Do not push price below the point where the factory can hold the spec and still make money.
conditions: Repeat orders of the same product, especially in price-competitive categories.
fails_when: Factories under tight, frequent third-party testing with clear penalties, where fade is caught early.

claim: Under CIF the seller only has to insure at the minimum level, Institute Cargo Clauses (C), while CIP requires the broader Clauses (A); ask for (A) cover or insure the cargo yourself.
body: Incoterms 2020 kept two different insurance levels. CIF, the sea-only rule, still requires only Institute Cargo Clauses (C), the narrowest standard cover, which pays for major events such as fire, sinking or a vessel collision but not for most theft, water damage or rough handling. CIP, the any-mode rule, now requires Clauses (A), which is close to all risks. The parties can agree a different level in either rule. Why it matters: a buyer who takes a CIF quote may assume the goods are fully insured when they are not, and under CIF the risk passes to the buyer once the goods are on board in the origin port, so any loss at sea is the buyer's problem with only the cover the seller chose. How to apply it: if you buy CIF, write in the PO that cover must be Institute Cargo Clauses (A) for 110% of the invoice value, and ask for the policy or certificate with the shipping documents. Or buy FOB or FCA and take cargo insurance through your own forwarder or insurer. Also check all costs in article A9/B9, where Incoterms 2020 lists every cost each party pays.

fails_when: You already hold an annual cargo policy that covers all your shipments, or the contract sets a different cover level.

claim: China's Dalian Commodity Exchange trades PP, LLDPE and PVC futures and, since 28 October 2025, monthly average price versions, a ready reference for index-linked plastic part quotes from Chinese factories.
body: Most plastic consumer goods made in China use polypropylene (PP), polyethylene (PE) or PVC, and Chinese moulders buy them at domestic prices. The Dalian Commodity Exchange lists physically delivered futures for all three. On 28 October 2025 it added monthly average price futures for LLDPE, PVC and PP, which settle on the average price across the contract month, approved by the China Securities Regulatory Commission. An average over a month is exactly the kind of reference a supply contract can use. How to apply it: for each moulded part, note the resin type and the resin share of the part cost from your should-cost. Agree with the factory that the resin share moves with the Dalian monthly average for that resin, say for the month before the PO, while labour, machine time and margin stay fixed for the year. Example: resin is 30% of the part cost and the PP monthly average rises 10%, so the part price rises 3%. Use the same rule for falls. This turns open-ended price-rise talks into a formula both sides can check.

claim: Build high and low cost cases from volatility: for a random-walk price, the h-month band is plus or minus c x sigma x square root of h, with c = 1.28 for 80% and 1.96 for 95%.
body: For a price where the latest value is the best simple forecast (the naive method), uncertainty grows with the forecast horizon. Hyndman and Athanasopoulos give the rule for the naive (last value) method: the forecast standard deviation h steps ahead is the one-step residual standard deviation times the square root of h. A prediction interval is the forecast plus or minus c times that standard deviation, with c = 1.28 for an 80% interval and 1.96 for 95%. How to apply it to a COGS forecast: (1) take 24 to 36 months of the index for each BOM line; (2) compute monthly percent changes and their standard deviation, say 3%; (3) for a six-month horizon, sigma is 3% x square root of 6 = 7.3%; (4) the 80% band is about plus or minus 9.4% and the 95% band about plus or minus 14.4%. Base case: latest price, or the World Bank forecast if you trust it. High and low cases: the band edges. Then pass each line's case through its share of FOB and its lag to get base, high and low unit COGS. Use the 80% band for planning prices and the 95% band for cash buffers.
conditions: Forecasting cost lines driven by traded prices (resin, metals, cotton, freight, exchange rates) 3 to 12 months ahead.
fails_when: Prices with strong trend or seasonality (use drift or seasonal methods), or after a shock that changes volatility.

claim: Set a tolerance on every measurement: one shirt brand allows plus or minus 0.4 in on chest width, 0.5 in on lengths and 0.3 in on collar and cuffs, doubling for circumferences.
body: A measurement with no tolerance cannot be failed fairly at inspection, and a tolerance that is too wide shows up as size returns. Proper Cloth publishes its working tolerances. Shirts: chest, midsection, bottom and yoke width plus or minus 0.4 in; sleeve width, collar and cuff 0.3 in; centre back length, centre front length and sleeve length 0.5 in. Jackets: chest width 0.4 in; most other points, including shoulder, sleeve length and centre back length, 0.3 in. Pants: hip, thigh and back rise 0.4 in; waist, knee, leg opening and front rise 0.3 in; total rise 0.7 in; inseam 0.5 in. Circumference tolerances are double the width tolerance (shirt chest circumference plus or minus 0.8 in). Variation comes from cutting and sewing, fabric and washes, and from how people measure, so define each point of measure with a diagram and method. How to apply: copy this structure into your spec sheet, with tighter limits on small areas (neck, cuff) and wider ones on stretch knits, and give the inspector the full table so out-of-tolerance pieces are logged as defects.

body: US duty and MPF are charged on the transaction value, which leaves out international freight and insurance, while the UK and EU charge on a value that includes them. Build the US sheet like this. Worked example, one ocean shipment of 2,000 units at $10 FOB = $20,000. Ocean freight and origin charges $2,400, insurance $60. Duty stack for a Chinese product with a 7% general rate, 25% Section 301 and 12.5% forced labor duty = 44.5% x $20,000 = $8,900. MPF = 0.3464% x $20,000 = $69.28 (between the $34.58 floor and $670.86 cap). HMF = 0.125% x $20,000 = $25. Broker entry and ISF fees, say $185 (get your own quote). Port to warehouse delivery $600. Total $32,239.28, so $16.12 per unit landed against $10 FOB. Run the same sheet for each origin and mode: air removes HMF but raises freight; a Vietnam origin would pay 12.5% added duty plus its general rate, with no China lists. claim: Ask a Chinese supplier for a letter of credit only on orders of about USD 30,000 or more, state it from first contact, and list an inspection certificate among the required documents.
body: Bank fees for a letter of credit are much higher than for a wire, so it only makes sense on larger orders, about USD 30,000 and up. Chinese exporters are less likely to accept an L/C for a one-off deal, so the tactic is to contact many potential suppliers, say up front that you always pay the first order by L/C, and get acceptance in writing before samples. Documents to require: commercial invoice, packing list, certificate of origin, bill of lading and an inspection certificate from the inspection firm you choose. The inspection certificate is the key one, because without it the bank pays against shipping papers even if the goods are faulty. Avoid 'soft' clauses that depend on your own approval; suppliers see them as a way for you to avoid paying and will refuse. Why it helps you: you avoid sending a down payment that is lost if the factory fails to perform, and a major bank in the middle reassures the factory. Small discrepancies in documents are common, and you can waive them, which sometimes gives room to negotiate.

claim: Plan Chinese New Year as 2 to 4 weeks lost: order in mid-December to cover sales to 1 April plus 15 to 30 days extra safety stock, and inspect the first post-holiday shipments more closely.
body: The legal holiday is about a week, but most factories close for about two weeks and some for four. Workers leave early, many do not come back, and the first runs after the break are made by new staff, while component suppliers restart late and hold up finished goods. A sourcing veteran's dated plan: build a material plan through 1 May; in mid-December order enough to cover sales through 1 April plus 15 to 30 days of extra safety stock, shipped before the shutdown; by 15 January place firm orders for top-priority items for production through 1 May, and give the factory estimated needs through 1 July as a blanket order. Many buyers aim for December shipment rather than January, because a late January shipment can slip to March. How to apply it for 2027 (holiday 5 to 13 February): the plan was written for a 10 February New Year, so use the same dates a few days earlier, ordering by mid-December 2026 and firming priority orders by about 10 January. Raise inspection one level above normal for each supplier, prefer a during-production check before the holiday so there is time to fix faults, and inspect the first batches after it closely.

fails_when: Suppliers in countries without the holiday, or products held in large buffer stock already.

claim: Time a during-production inspection to the first finished output, not a calendar date: on a 30-day, 20,000-piece order with first units on day 8, day 12 is right.
body: Inspect too early and the first units are worse than average and the factory has not done its own checks; inspect too late and the damage is done. Large Asian orders often show finished goods only one to two weeks in, and by the time 50% is finished another 30% may already be cut and in process, so a defect found then can affect 80% of the order. The author's rule of thumb works for about 80% of consumer goods: the factory knows the product, and the first finished units appear within 10 days of starting. In his worked example, a 20,000-piece order takes 30 days, the first finished units come off on day 8, and about 600 units are ready 4 days later, so the DUPRO goes in on day 12. What it checks: production activity and updated planning, conformity to specs, visual defects against AQL limits, and simple on-site function tests. How to apply: ask the factory for the date the first finished units leave the line, then book the DUPRO a few days after, once a few hundred units exist. Never let it replace the final inspection, since factories can hide problems and packing often arrives late.

claim: Use general level II by default, level III after recent quality problems or for high-value goods, level I only for suppliers with a clean record, and S1 to S4 for slow or destructive tests.
body: The inspection level sets how big the sample is for a given lot, so it is the main cost and risk dial in an inspection booking. For a 5,000-piece order the sample is 80 at level I, 200 at level II and 315 at level III; at 40,000 pieces it is 200, 500 and 800. The special levels give tiny samples for checks that take long or destroy the product: at 5,000 pieces S-1 is 5, S-2 is 8, S-3 is 20 and S-4 is 32. How to apply: book level II for normal visual and workmanship checks. Move to level III for the next lots after a supplier fails or after returns spike, for high-value items, or for small orders where the inspection takes a full day anyway, so the extra sample costs nothing. Drop to level I only once a supplier has passed most past inspections; the author warns that choosing it just to save time and money is very risky. Put function tests, drop tests, fabric weight checks and other destructive tests under an S level (S-2 or S-3 is typical) and say so in the checklist, so the inspector does not either skip them or destroy 200 units. Container loading checks also use special levels.

claim: A purchase order is not a full supply contract; pay a China-business lawyer once for a master agreement, then change only the exhibits (specs, price, dates) for each order.
body: Most small brands buy on a PO or a proforma invoice and a chat thread. That leaves out the terms that matter when things go wrong: quality standard, inspection rights, tooling ownership, penalties and where disputes are heard. The fix is cheaper than it sounds. Have a lawyer who knows Chinese business law draft one enforceable master agreement, in Chinese with an English translation. After that, each order needs only new exhibits: the spec sheet, the price list, quantities and ship dates. Its main value is leverage, not lawsuits. A factory that knows you can enforce in China takes your quality and date complaints more seriously, and you rarely need to sue. How to apply it: sign the master agreement before the first bulk order and before you pay any tooling. Make every PO say it is issued under that agreement, list the exhibit versions it uses, and keep signed and chopped copies of both. Never wire a down payment before the factory confirms it understands the requirements, never to a personal account, and never to an account name that differs from the supplier without a written explanation.

New suppliers miss more often because the product and your standards are new to them. A sourcing veteran's buffer is 3 to 4 extra weeks in your own plan for a new supplier and about 2 weeks for a regular one, on top of the total lead time to the ship date. Beyond price, the terms to agree before the first order are: total lead time and ship date; the Incoterm; IP protection; your right to inspect at the approved factory during production; quality standards and certifications; staged payment; and the OEM terms people forget, namely who pays the first inspection and lab tests, late-shipment penalties, chargebacks, control over price increases, compensation if the supplier cannot deliver, and your right to refuse orders. Put the listed terms in the master agreement or the first PO.

claim: A small buyer can often get the balance paid after shipment but before the original bill of lading is released, a 10 to 20% deposit on non-custom goods, and better terms after one or two orders.

First, on FOB sea shipments, pay the balance after the goods are on the vessel but before the factory releases the original bill of lading; you still control payment timing and the factory still controls the cargo until paid, so both sides are covered. Ask for this at the start, not later. Second, for products that are not heavily customised and that the factory could sell to someone else if you cancelled, the deposit can drop to 10 to 20%. claim: Price the payment terms you are asking for: value of a later balance = order value x share moved x days moved / 365 x your annual cost of cash.
body: Paying in full before goods ship ties up working capital for the whole of production and transit, which this sourcing veteran calls a hidden cost of buying from China. Putting a number on it tells you how much price you could trade for better terms. Formula: value = order value x share of payment moved later x days moved / 365 x your annual cost of cash (your loan or card rate, or the return you get on ad spend if you are cash-limited). Example: a USD 40,000 order, 70% balance moved from before shipment to 35 days later (sea transit plus clearance), with cash costing 15% a year: 40,000 x 0.70 x 35 / 365 x 0.15 = about USD 400, or 1% of the order. How to apply it: if the factory offers 1% off for paying before shipment, the two are roughly equal and you should take whichever lowers risk. If cash is your constraint because stockouts cost sales, use a higher rate. Use the same sum to judge a lower deposit: moving 10% of the order forward by 60 days is worth less than most buyers think.

You then cannot move production without paying again, which weakens every later negotiation on price, quality or dates. The 30% funds materials and is rarely returned if the order goes wrong, so call it a down payment, not a deposit, and only send it once the factory clearly understands the specification. The leverage question is when the 70% is paid. If it is due before the goods leave, the factory has been paid in full before you know whether the goods are right. Better versions, in order of buyer protection: 70% after a third-party inspection passes; 70% after shipment against a copy of the bill of lading; and, where you have strong competition between suppliers, a 20/50/30 split with 30% paid after delivery to your warehouse. Avoid 100% prepayment, which removes any reason for the factory to fix problems or keep your ship date. A good factory comes back with options: a different material, a simpler finish, a process step that can be dropped, a change in packing, or a higher quantity, each with its saving. That shows it understands its cost structure and will be open about trade-offs. A factory that pleads and then simply accepts the lower price has to find that margin somewhere, and the usual place is the spec, quietly, a few orders later. claim: When your sales are steady, trade a committed order schedule for a fixed pricing formula in an OEM agreement, so price moves only with agreed inputs rather than each new quote.

A buyer with reliable volumes can offer something worth more than a bigger single order: a schedule the factory can plan labour and materials around. With a lawyer, set it out in an OEM agreement: fixed or minimum order quantities per quarter, and a pricing formula, for example a base price that moves only with an agreed material index or exchange rate band. claim: After a failed inspection, the re-inspection and any aborted visit should be at the supplier's cost: pay the inspector yourself and deduct the fee from the balance with a debit note.

Standard practice in Asian sourcing is that the buyer pays the first inspection and the supplier pays every re-inspection after a legitimate rejection, plus any visit aborted because the goods or references were not ready as promised. The simplest way to collect is not to ask the supplier to pay the inspection firm, which invites stalling (asking for an original stamped invoice, paying only in RMB, waiting for the boss), but to pay it yourself and issue a debit note that is deducted from the next payment, usually the balance. If you do let the supplier pay directly, require payment in advance. Suppliers often offer to pay for one man-day only; refuse if the re-check genuinely needs two, because one inspector cannot do two days of work in one. State it as a fixed term, not a negotiation.

claim: The most reliable reference for an inspector is an approved sample you forward to the inspection company yourself, because a sample left at the factory can be swapped or degraded.
body: An inspection compares production units to a reference. If the reference sits at the factory, the factory controls it, and the temptation to swap it for something closer to bulk can decide pass or fail. Options from best to weakest: have the factory send several samples, approve them, and courier a few to the inspection company's local office; check the production launch yourself, sign a sample and send the inspector a photo; send samples to the factory in a sealed package to be opened only by the inspector; courier units from your own stock if they are identical to what you ordered; for bulky goods such as furniture, send cut pieces so the inspector can compare material and feel. Readers add practical rules: tag and stamp golden samples permanently and note any flaws on the tag, store them dry, dark and bagged, ask the factory to hold several sets because samples get dirty, and replace retained samples about every 6 months. How to apply: on every inspection booking, state where the approved sample is and how it is sealed, and ask for photos of the sample beside production units in the report.

claim: An inspector should open at least the square root of the total export cartons, picked at random from all parts of the stack in a non-patterned number series.

The fix: the inspector picks at least the square root of the total carton count (500 cartons means at least 23), chooses carton numbers with no arithmetic pattern (for example 3, 10, 17, 23, 32), takes them from the top, bottom, sides and centre of the pile, and watches workers carry them so none are swapped on the way. Units for the AQL sample are then drawn across those cartons. How to apply: write the square-root rule into your inspection checklist, and ask for a photo of the full stack and of each opened carton number in the report. If goods are not stacked so cartons can be reached, the report should say so, and you should treat the result with caution or rebook. On re-inspections after a failure, open more cartons than the first time, since the factory knows which ones were checked.

Keep the higher cluster only if you want above-average quality. Pay for factory audits once you are down to one or two candidates. claim: EU customs value is the price paid plus transport and insurance up to the point goods enter the EU, plus commissions, packing and assists; transport after entry, buying commission and import duties are excluded.
body: The EU uses the WTO transaction value method, which the Commission says covers about 95% of EU trade. Start from the price actually paid or payable for the goods sold for export to the EU. Add, if not already in the price: selling commission and brokerage, cost of containers and packing, assists (goods and services you supplied free or cheaply to make the goods, such as moulds or artwork), royalties paid as a condition of sale, proceeds of resale that go back to the seller, and transport and related costs up to the point of entry into the EU. Leave out transport after entry, interest charges, import duties and taxes, assembly after entry and buying commission. So, unlike the US, EU duty is charged on a CIF-style value: on FOB terms add the ocean or air freight and insurance to the EU border. Steps: get freight invoices that show the leg to the EU border separately from EU inland delivery, and keep mould and royalty records with the PO.

claim: Plan 5 to 7 sample rounds per new garment style: proto, fit, size set, salesman, performance test, pre-production, sealed, top of production and shipment samples, with bulk only after size set and PP approval.
body: Each sample answers one question, and skipping one usually moves the problem into bulk. Proto: does the style and look work (often three made: two for you, one kept by the factory). Fit: does it fit your base size; expect several rounds. Size set: does grading work across sizes; three of each size in final fabric and finishes. Salesman (SMS): finished units in approved sizes for photos and selling. Garment performance test (GPT): seam strength, seam slippage, colourfastness and wash fastness before bulk. Pre-production (PP): the factory's first run on the production line in final materials; bulk starts only after you approve it. Sealed sample: the approved PP tagged as the locked standard (gold seal for approved, red for rejected). Top of production (TOP): pulled from early bulk, including packaging, to confirm bulk matches PP. Shipment sample: checks folding and packing before you release shipping. 3D samples can cut early rounds but take time and money to set up. How to apply: put the sample plan, each round's turnaround and who pays into the development timeline before quoting a launch date, and approve each round in writing against the tech pack revision number.

claim: The World Bank Pink Sheet gives free monthly prices for cotton, natural rubber, plywood, sawnwood, aluminium, copper, zinc, nickel, tin and iron ore, but no steel, plastic resin or paper pulp series.
body: The Pink Sheet is the easiest free monthly source for several common BOM inputs, but you need to know what each line really is. Cotton is the Cotlook A index, a Far East delivered price for middling 1-3/32 inch cotton, close to what Asian spinners pay. Natural rubber is the Singapore exchange RSS3 and TSR20 grades, relevant to soles, mats and elastic. Aluminium, copper, zinc, nickel, tin and lead are London Metal Exchange cash prices for primary metal. Iron ore is 62% Fe fines delivered China. Plywood is a Tokyo wholesale price for a 3-ply sheet; sawnwood is Malaysian and African hardwood. How to apply it: map each BOM line to the closest series and note the gap. Metals in the Pink Sheet are raw metal, not sheet, extrusion or finished hardware, so a 10% move in aluminium moves an extruded part by less. There is no steel, plastic resin, polyester or pulp line, so take those from a producer price index or an exchange instead. Appraisal costs measure conformance: checking incoming material, set-ups and products against specs, quality audits and supplier rating. In its example, $700 of a $1,000 price is indexed, so each 1% change in the index is worth $7. A 5.2% rise adds $36.40, giving $1,036.40, against $1,052 if the whole price were indexed. For a garment where fabric is half the FOB, a 6% fabric move is worth 3%. Add up each line's share times its own index move to get the expected quote change, and compare it with what the supplier asks. Recompute the shares once a year, because a big material move changes its own share.
