claim: A US general-use product covered by a CPSC rule needs a General Certificate of Conformity from testing or a reasonable testing programme, but no accepted lab or tracking label.
body: Many adult products are not regulated by any CPSC rule, but many are: mattresses, bike helmets, certain textiles for flammability, products under the Federal Hazardous Substances Act, and others listed in CPSC's regulated products table. For those, the domestic manufacturer or importer must issue a General Certificate of Conformity (GCC) based on testing or a reasonable testing programme. Unlike children's products, the testing does not have to be done at a CPSC-accepted lab, and tracking labels are not required. The GCC goes to retailers and distributors and to the government on request. Separately, every business has a duty to report to CPSC when it learns a product may be defective with a substantial risk of injury, breaks a rule, was choked on by a child with serious results, or is the subject of certain lawsuits, whether or not any rule applies. How to apply: check CPSC's regulated products table (cpsc.gov/certify) for each SKU. If a rule applies, keep the test report and issue a GCC naming each rule. If none applies, keep a note saying so, because from July 2026 imports need a certificate filing or a disclaimer at entry.

claim: US children's products (age 12 and under) need third-party tests at a CPSC-accepted lab, a Children's Product Certificate, permanent tracking labels, lead under 100 ppm and paint under 90 ppm.

Then list every rule that applies; the common ones are total lead content in any accessible part of 100 ppm or less, lead in paint and surface coatings of 90 ppm or less, small parts (banned for under 3s, warning label for ages 3 to under 6), the toy safety standard ASTM F963 for toys, the phthalates ban for toys and child care articles, and durable infant product rules with a product registration card for cribs, strollers, high chairs and similar. Then test every rule at a CPSC-accepted third-party lab (find one in CPSC's lab search), issue a Children's Product Certificate from those results, give it to every retailer and distributor and to CPSC on request, and put permanent tracking information on the product and its packaging. Retesting is needed periodically (usually yearly) and after any material change. Small batch manufacturers with revenue below about 1 million USD who meet other conditions can get relief from some third-party testing. How to apply: get a lab quote listing each rule before you place the PO, and budget the test cost per style and colourway.

claim: Drewry's World Container Index is a weekly spot rate in US dollars per 40ft on 8 east-west lanes, port to port, including fuel and other carrier surcharges but excluding inland haulage, documents and customs fees.
body: The WCI is the most quoted free weekly benchmark for container freight, so know what is inside it before you plug it into a landed cost. Lanes: Shanghai to Rotterdam, Genoa, Los Angeles and New York, plus Rotterdam to Shanghai, Los Angeles to Shanghai, New York to Rotterdam and Rotterdam to New York. Rates are container yard to container yard and include surcharges such as bunker fuel adjustments, the EU emissions surcharge, currency, peak season, port congestion and canal surcharges. They exclude inland transport, documentation, booking and customs clearance fees. Data come from forwarders and NVOCCs reporting rates agreed with carriers, valid for 7 days to a month; quotes and bids are not used. For each lane, rates more than 30% above or below the median are dropped. The composite weights lanes by volume. How to apply it: use the lane matching your route as the freight line driver in your landed cost model, then add origin charges, destination charges, drayage and customs brokerage from your forwarder's invoices as separate fixed lines. If your contract rate sits well below spot, watch the gap: contract rates tend to follow spot at the next renewal.

fails_when: Lanes it does not cover (for example Asia to Australia or India origin), LCL shipments, or long fixed contract rates.

claim: Price packaging cube in money: at Drewry's 12 Nov 2026 Shanghai to Rotterdam rate of $3,504 per 40ft, a container of 6,000 units carries $0.58 of ocean freight each, and a 10% smaller carton that fits 6,600 saves about $0.05.
body: Shrinking the master carton or retail box is one of the few cost-downs that touches no material spec, and the public freight index lets you value it. Take the lane's weekly WCI rate: on 12 Nov 2026 Drewry put Shanghai to Rotterdam at $3,504, Shanghai to Los Angeles at $7,416 and Shanghai to New York at $9,020 per 40ft. If 6,000 units fit, ocean freight to Rotterdam is $3,504 / 6,000 = $0.58 a unit. Cut carton volume 10% so 6,600 fit and it drops to $0.53. To New York the same change is worth about $0.14 a unit. How to apply it: in your BOM, add a packaging line for each packing level (retail box, insert, inner pack, share of master carton) and a freight-per-unit line driven by units per container. Then test options: fold-flat or nested designs, less void fill, a retail box sized to the product, more units per master carton. Note the index covers only port to port spot freight; add origin and destination charges and duty to get landed cost. Check that a smaller box does not raise damage claims: run a drop test before switching.

claim: Expect raw and intermediate input moves to reach consumer goods factory prices slowly and partly: ECB estimates about half a year for the first effect, with only about a quarter of the move passed through.
body: When resin, metal or fabric prices jump, a finished goods quote rarely jumps by the same percentage on the next PO. ECB economists, using euro area data from 1999 to 2019, estimate that changes in intermediate goods prices take around six months to reach producer prices of non-food consumer goods, with relatively low pass-through of around one quarter at that stage. It then takes at least another year and a half for producer price moves to pass fully into consumer prices. They note the lag is longer where firms use long-term contracts, fixed prices or hedging. How to apply it: in your COGS forecast, phase input moves in rather than applying them at once. A simple default with no BOM data: apply about a quarter of a broad input price move to the finished goods quote, starting about two quarters later. With a BOM, do better: apply each input move only to that input's share of the FOB price, on the timing your contract or supplier's buying pattern implies. Use the same lag in reverse: when inputs fall, push for a price cut about two quarters later, because the supplier's costs will have fallen by then.
conditions: Consumer goods with several inputs and some labour; forecasting over the next 6 to 18 months.
fails_when: Products where one raw material is most of the cost (pass-through is higher and faster), or contracts with monthly index clauses.

body: For a euro-based store, the ECB reference rates are the cleanest free daily series to put in a cost model. They cover 29 currencies against the euro, including the US dollar, yuan, Indian rupee, pound and yen, and come from a daily check among European central banks at about 14:10 CET, published around 16:00 CET on each working day except TARGET holidays. History downloads as CSV or XML. The ECB says the rates are for information only and discourages using them for transactions, so the rate your bank or payment provider gives you will be worse. How to apply it: keep a dated log of the EUR/USD and EUR/CNY reference rates on each PO date and payment date. Convert supplier quotes at the reference rate, then add your provider's real margin, which you can measure by comparing a few past payments with the reference rate on the same day. For forecasts, use the current rate as the base case, and the high and low bands from the rate's own past volatility. Most Asian factories quote in US dollars, so EUR/USD is usually the rate that matters most.

claim: Origin charges (export clearance, CFS fees, document and filing fees) sit with the seller under FOB but with you under EXW, so compare forwarder quotes only line by line on the same Incoterm.
body: Origin charges pay for work done before the shipment leaves the origin port or airport: export customs clearance, container freight station fees for LCL, the fee to issue and send the bill of lading, and security filing fees such as AMS for US-bound cargo. Under FOB the seller normally pays these up to loading, so they will not appear on your forwarder's bill. Under EXW your forwarder bills them to you. Two freight quotes can therefore look far apart only because one includes origin charges and the other leaves them with the supplier. How to apply it: ask each forwarder for a line-by-line quote split into origin, main freight and destination charges, and state the Incoterm you buy on. Agree with the supplier in writing which origin costs are in its price before the first shipment. Then add the lines to your landed cost per unit. If a supplier's FOB price rises when you ask for FCA or EXW, check that the change matches the origin charges it no longer pays or newly pays.

claim: US apparel needs a permanent care label with at least one full washing or dry-cleaning method, warnings against any harmful step, and test or other reliable evidence behind it before sale.
body: Care labels are a spec item the factory cannot write for you. Under 16 CFR 423, manufacturers and importers must attach a label that stays legible for the garment's useful life and can be seen or easily found at the point of sale (if packaging hides it, repeat the care information on the package or a hang tag). It needs a washing or a dry-cleaning instruction; if both work, one is enough, and if neither is safe the label must say so. A washing instruction states hand or machine wash and a water temperature unless hot water up to 145 F is safe; machine or other drying and a temperature unless high heat is safe; ironing only if regularly needed, with a temperature unless a hot iron is safe; and 'No bleach' or 'Only non-chlorine bleach' if all bleaches are not safe. Warn against any step a consumer or cleaner might reasonably take that would cause harm, using words such as Do not, No or Only. ASTM D5489 symbols may replace or support words. You must hold a reasonable basis, such as tests on the garment or its components, before sale. How to apply: have your lab or factory wash-test the PP sample against the label you plan, and put the final care text and symbols in the tech pack's label section.

claim: Since 13 December 2024, a consumer product sold into the EU or Northern Ireland needs a responsible economic operator established there, named with a postal address on the product, packaging, parcel or paperwork.
body: Under Article 16 of EU Regulation 2023/988 (GPSR), a product may only be placed on the market if an economic operator established in the EU (or Northern Ireland) carries the compliance tasks. In order, that is the manufacturer if it is established there; an authorised representative the manufacturer appoints in writing; the importer if there is no EU manufacturer or representative; and, as a last resort, a fulfilment service provider. Established means a real registered office or permanent place of business, not a PO box. Its name, registered trade name or trademark and contact details, including a postal address, must appear on the product or its packaging, the parcel or an accompanying document such as a receipt or despatch note. Its tasks include holding technical documentation for market surveillance authorities for 10 years after the product is placed on the market, cooperating with them, and making sure accident reports are made where Article 20 requires. How to apply: a non-EU brand selling direct to EU consumers should appoint an authorised representative (or agree the role with its EU 3PL), add the representative's details to labels or the packing slip, and list them on each product listing.

claim: Under the EU GPSR a manufacturer must do an internal risk assessment and technical file before sale, put a batch or serial number on each product, and give its postal and email address and local-language safety information.
body: The GPSR makes paperwork and traceability the price of entry, even for simple products with no CE marking. Before placing a product on the market, the manufacturer must carry out an internal risk assessment and draw up technical documentation. Each product must be identifiable, for example by a type, batch or serial number, on the product or, if size or nature prevents it, on the packaging or an accompanying document. The manufacturer's name, registered trade name or trademark and postal and electronic address (plus a single contact point if different) must be shown. Clear instructions and safety information must be given in a language consumers in that country can easily understand, where needed. Manufacturers and importers must act immediately if they believe a product is dangerous, including reporting through the EU Safety Business Gateway. How to apply: build a one-file technical folder per product (risk assessment, test reports, BOM, label artwork, supplier details), add a batch code to the tech pack's label section so every production run is traceable, and translate safety warnings for each country you ship to.

claim: UK customs value includes freight and insurance up to the UK port or airport, including peak season and congestion surcharges; UK inland transport and demurrage after arrival can be left out if shown separately.
body: The UK, like the EU, charges duty on a CIF-style value, unlike the US. HMRC says to include all transport costs up to the place of introduction: the UK port for sea, the point the UK border is crossed for air, and the delivery address for post. That covers freight, insurance in transit, loading and handling, container and terminal charges abroad, inland transport in the export country, bunker and currency adjustments, and peak season, security, war risk and UK port congestion surcharges. You can exclude demurrage caused by delay after arrival, UK terminal costs if charged separately, and transport inside the UK if it is shown separately. On ex-works terms the whole freight from the factory is included; on FOB terms only the freight from the export port. For air, only part of the air transport cost is included, using HMRC's published percentages. Steps: ask your forwarder for invoices that split costs to the UK border from UK-side costs, because without that split HMRC will expect you to include them all, and duty is charged on them.

claim: Score suppliers out of 100 on quality, on-time delivery, lead-time cut and inventory turns, 25 each; 98 to 100% on time earns full delivery points, under 90% means probation, and the top two split volume about 70/30.
body: A former operations executive's scorecard leaves price out on purpose, so the scores show performance rather than who is cheapest. Quality: rejects per million received, monthly and as a rolling three months. Delivery: (deliveries minus late deliveries) / deliveries. On-time bands: 98 to 100% scores 25 and marks a certified supplier; 95 to 97% scores 20 and is the minimum to stay qualified; 93 to 94% scores 10 and, after three months running, needs an improvement plan within 30 days; 90 to 92% scores 5 and, after two months, needs an action plan to reach 95%; under 90% scores 0 and means probation with a plan due in 15 days. Lead time: points for cutting it, 25 for a cut over 50%. Inventory turns: points for improvement on last year. How to apply it for a small brand: track on-time against the ship date in the PO, and defects from inspection reports, for each supplier each month. Review the card with the supplier every quarter. Where two suppliers make the same item, give about 70% of volume to the higher scorer and 30% to the other, and let them know volume follows the score.

claim: US children's products must be retested at a CPSC-accepted lab at least yearly, or every 2 years with a production testing plan, or every 3 years with ISO/IEC 17025 lab testing during production.
body: Passing once is not enough for a product you keep making. Under 16 CFR 1107.21, a manufacturer of a children's product in continuing production must keep testing samples at a third-party lab on a schedule set by its plan. With only a periodic testing plan, the interval may not exceed one year. With a written production testing plan (in-house or other production checks that give high assurance between lab tests), third-party periodic testing can be at least once every two years. If production testing is done by an ISO/IEC 17025-accredited lab using the same methods as certification, third-party periodic tests can be at least once every three years. The interval can be set by time, number of units or another method, as long as the maximum is not exceeded. Separate rules require retesting after a material change in design, materials or supplier. How to apply: for each children's SKU, log the last test date and the next due date in your product master, and trigger a new test whenever the factory changes a material, colourant or component supplier, even if the style number stays the same.

fails_when: One-off short runs (CPSC says runs under a year have no periodic testing duty, though each new run needs certification), or non-children's products.

3 years: with ISO/IEC 17025 lab production testing

claim: A US firm must report to CPSC within 24 hours once information reasonably supports a reportable hazard; any investigation should take no more than 10 days, and staff reports should reach the decision maker within 5.
body: The reporting clock is the rule that small brands most often miss. Under section 15(b) of the CPSA, the duty can arise from the first information about a possible defect, a rule breach or an unreasonable risk; you do not need full proof. If you are unsure, you may investigate, but that investigation should not exceed 10 days unless you can show more time is reasonable. Information known to any employee who could appreciate it counts as known to the firm, and under ordinary circumstances 5 days is the maximum for it to reach the CEO or the person responsible for reporting. Once the information reasonably supports a reportable conclusion, report within 24 hours. Weekends and holidays are excluded from the time periods in this part. How to apply: set a rule in your support desk that any ticket, review or return mentioning injury, burn, fire, choking, shock or a broken part that could hurt someone is escalated to one named person the same day, logged with a date, and assessed within 10 days. Monitor reviews and SaferProducts.gov for your products too.

fails_when: Complaints about cosmetic or comfort issues with no plausible injury risk or rule breach.

claim: A store selling its own brand is responsible for Prop 65 warnings itself; suppliers can pass the duty to retailers only by written notice renewed every year and updated within 90 days of a chemical change.
body: California splits the warning duty along the supply chain. Manufacturers, producers, importers and distributors comply either by labelling the product or by sending the retailer's authorised agent a written notice that names the product, says it may expose people to a listed chemical and includes all warning materials, including warnings for internet sales. The retailer must confirm receipt, and the notice must be renewed every year while the product is sold in California; a new notice is due within 90 days when a different chemical or endpoint is added. A retail seller is responsible itself when it sells under a brand it or an affiliate owns or licenses, adds a listed chemical, covers or alters a warning, ignores a notice it received, or knows of the exposure and no upstream party has a California presence. For a direct-to-consumer brand that imports its own product, all of these roles sit with you. Upstream parties can also allocate the duty by written agreement. How to apply: if you wholesale to other stores, send the annual written notice and keep the receipts; if you sell your own brand, label the product and your product pages yourself.

fails_when: Products needing no warning, or where a written agreement places the duty elsewhere.

claim: For online sales into California, a Prop 65 warning must sit on the product page, behind a link labelled WARNING on that page, or be shown prominently before checkout completes.
body: A label on the box is not enough when the buyer cannot see the box before paying. Under 27 CCR 25602(b), an internet sale needs the warning content from section 25603 delivered in one of three ways: a warning on the product display page; a clearly marked hyperlink on the product display page using the word WARNING, CA WARNING or CALIFORNIA WARNING that opens the warning; or a warning otherwise prominently displayed to the buyer before the purchase is completed. It is not prominent if the buyer must search the general site content to find it. If the product label uses the short-form warning, the website may use the same short-form text. Catalogues need the warning next to the item so it clearly applies to it. For internet purchases before 1 January 2028, a retail seller is not responsible for posting an updated warning until 60 days after it receives the new warning or notice from upstream. How to apply: for each SKU that needs a warning, add it as a product metafield shown on the product page (or a WARNING link) and confirm it appears for California addresses before payment.

claim: Since 1 January 2025 the Prop 65 short-form warning must name at least one listed chemical; the old chemical-free short form is allowed only on products made and labelled before 1 January 2028.
body: The short-form warning was popular because it fitted small labels without naming a chemical. The 2025 amendment to 27 CCR 25603 keeps the short form but adds the chemical: each short-form option now reads along the lines of a cancer or reproductive-harm risk from exposure to the named chemical, plus www.P65Warnings.ca.gov. All warnings still need the yellow equilateral triangle with a black exclamation point, outlined in black, to the left of the text and at least as tall as the word WARNING, which must be in bold capitals (CA WARNING or CALIFORNIA WARNING are also allowed). Full-length warnings must name one or more chemicals too. The legacy short form (for example Cancer, then the website) remains allowed for any product manufactured and labelled before 1 January 2028, whenever it is sold, so existing stock needs no relabelling. How to apply: ask your lab which listed chemical drives the warning for each SKU, update label artwork at the next packaging reprint, and have every new production run from 2028 carry the new short form or a full warning.

claim: Imports that arrive without a required US origin marking owe an extra 10% ad valorem duty unless marked, exported or destroyed under customs supervision before liquidation.
body: A missing 'Made in' is not just a relabel job. Under 19 USC 1304(i), an article not marked as required at importation is charged a duty of 10% of its value, on top of any other duty and even if the goods are otherwise duty free, and the duty cannot be remitted. The only ways out are to export it, destroy it, or mark it after import under customs supervision before the entry is liquidated, which means paying for warehouse labour and storage while it sits. Removing, covering or altering a required marking to hide the origin is a crime: up to 100,000 USD in fines and a year in prison for a first offence, and up to 250,000 USD for later ones. How to price the risk: on a 50,000 USD container, a missing marking costs 5,000 USD in marking duty, or the cost of a supervised relabel, before any delay. How to apply: make origin marking a major defect in your defect list and a line on every pre-shipment inspection checklist, and never ask a 3PL to cover origin labels with your own stickers.

fails_when: Articles exempt from marking under 19 USC 1304 exceptions or CBP's lists.

claim: China charges 13% VAT on most goods, so a 含税 (tax included) price carries domestic VAT that export sales normally do not; ask factories and 1688 sellers whether a price is 含税 or 不含税.
body: Under China's VAT Law, in force from 1 January 2026, the rate on sales of goods is 13%, with 9% on some goods and services. Exports are generally zero-rated. That gives Chinese suppliers two price bases: a domestic price that is often 含税 (tax included, with a VAT invoice), and an export price that should not carry domestic VAT. Prices on 1688, Alibaba's domestic wholesale market, are set for Chinese buyers and may be quoted either 含税 or 不含税 (tax excluded), so two listings for the same item can differ by the tax alone. Why it matters: if you compare a 含税 domestic price with a factory's export FOB price, or let an agent buy at a 含税 price for goods you export, you can overpay by up to the 13% VAT. How to apply it: on every quote ask 含税吗 (is tax included?) and whether the price is 出厂价 (ex-factory) or FOB. For export orders ask for the export price without domestic VAT. If you buy through a 1688 agent, ask the agent to show the seller's price basis and its own fee as separate lines.

claim: China's 2027 Spring Festival holiday runs 5 to 13 February, with Sundays 31 January and 14 February as make-up working days; National Day runs 1 to 7 October, with 26 September and 9 October worked.
body: The State Council's General Office sets the official holiday dates each autumn for the following year; the 2027 notice came out on 5 November 2026. Spring Festival is 9 days off, from Friday 5 February (Lunar New Year's Eve) to Saturday 13 February, with Sunday 31 January and Sunday 14 February worked instead. National Day, Golden Week, is 7 days, 1 to 7 October, with Sunday 26 September and Saturday 9 October worked. Labour Day is 1 to 5 May with Saturday 8 May worked. Why it matters: these are only the legal days. Factories stop well before Spring Festival and restart slowly after, and ports, trucking and inspection firms are busy on both sides of each break. How to apply it: put these dates in your purchasing calendar now. Work back from the shutdown to set the last date goods must pass inspection and leave the factory, then the last PO date using your full production lead time. Ask each supplier for its own closing and reopening dates in writing, since they are often longer than the official ones.

claim: Ocean freight per unit is container rate divided by units that fit: a 40ft high cube holds 76.2 cubic metres, 12.7% more than a 40ft standard (67.6), and two 20ft boxes (33.1 each) hold less than one 40ft.
body: For light, bulky consumer goods, the container fills by volume long before weight, so carton size sets freight per unit. ONE lists inside volume of 33.1 cubic metres for a 20ft dry, 67.6 for a 40ft and 76.2 for a 40ft high cube, with the high cube 2,695 mm tall inside versus 2,390. Max payloads are 28,330 kg, 26,840 kg and 28,800 kg. How to apply it: work out master carton volume (L x W x H in metres), how many cartons stack in the container in the best orientation, and units per carton. Freight per unit = all-in container cost / units loaded. Cartons never fill the nominal volume perfectly, so get a load plan from the forwarder rather than dividing 76.2 by carton volume. Rules: if you are volume-bound, ask for a 40ft high cube quote; the extra 12.7% space often costs little extra. If you are weight-bound (ceramics, metal, liquids), the 40ft standard hits its payload first, so compare per kilo. Avoid two 20ft containers in place of one 40ft: you get less space and usually pay more.

claim: State the inspection standard in the PO: ISO 2859-1 General Level II, AQL 0 for critical, 2.5 for major and 4.0 for minor defects; for a 4,000-unit lot that means 200 samples, reject at 11 major defects.
body: AQL is the most defective units allowed in a random sample before the whole batch fails. Inspection firms work to ISO 2859-1, the same tables as ANSI/ASQ Z1.4. The common consumer-goods default is General Inspection Level II with AQL 0 for critical defects (any safety or compliance failure fails the lot), 2.5 for major defects that would likely cause a return, and 4.0 for minor cosmetic ones; higher-risk products often use 1.0 for major. Worked example: a lot of 4,000 units at Level II gives code letter L and a sample of 200; at AQL 2.5 the lot passes with 10 or fewer major defects and fails at 11. How to apply it: write the standard, level and the three AQL numbers into the PO or quality agreement, attach a defect list that says what counts as critical, major and minor for your product, and state that a failed lot is reworked and re-inspected at the factory's cost before the balance is paid. Without this written in advance, an inspection report is only an opinion the factory can argue with.
conditions: Consumer products checked by random-sample inspection before shipment.
fails_when: Safety-critical, medical or child products that need tighter limits or full testing, or very small lots where sampling tables give little protection.

claim: At ISO 2859-1 general level II, a 3,201 to 10,000 unit lot is code letter L: inspect 200 units and reject at 11 majors (AQL 2.5) or 15 minors (AQL 4.0).
body: AQL sampling is a two-step lookup. Table 1 turns lot size and inspection level into a code letter; table 2 turns the letter into a sample size and an accept and reject number for each AQL. ANSI/ASQ Z1.4 and ISO 2859-1 use the same tables. The rows a store hits most often at general level II, normal inspection: 281 to 500 units is H, sample 50, accept 3 majors at 2.5 and 5 minors at 4.0. 501 to 1,200 is J, sample 80, accept 5 and 7. 1,201 to 3,200 is K, sample 125, accept 7 and 10. 3,201 to 10,000 is L, sample 200, accept 10 and 14. 10,001 to 35,000 is M, sample 315, accept 14 and 21. 35,001 to 150,000 is N, sample 500, accept 21 majors. Reject is always accept plus one. Count defective units, not defects, unless your contract says otherwise. How to apply: put the lot size (the whole PO quantity of that style, not one colour) into the calculator, write the level, AQLs and resulting sample into the PO and the inspection booking, and tell the inspector the lot is the full shipment quantity. If the sample is bigger than the lot, inspect every unit. Note how the sample grows much slower than the lot: 10,000 units needs 200 checks, 35,000 needs 315, so one big PO is cheaper to inspect per unit than several small ones.

fails_when: Lots under about 50 units (sampling gives little assurance; check all), medical or safety-critical goods needing tighter plans, or measurement-based checks that need variables sampling (ISO 3951).

claim: A pre-shipment inspection needs at least 80% of the order finished and packed; critical defects fail it outright, majors are judged against the AQL, and the report gives defect counts by class.
body: The procedure runs in a fixed order. Quantity check: the inspector counts finished and packed goods and cartons; if under 80% is finished and packed, the result is a fail or the visit is wasted. Workmanship: units from the random sample are checked for defects such as cracks, stains and chips, each classed critical, major or minor; any critical fails the lot, majors are compared to the AQL limit, minors pass if within their limit. Conformity: colour, materials and construction, dimensions, artwork and labels against your spec and approved sample. Function and on-site tests by category: for textiles pull, fatigue and stretch tests, fabric weight and composition, seam strength and stitches per inch; for hard goods sharp edges, pinch points, loose screws and weak hinges; for electrical goods hi-pot, earth continuity and similar safety checks. Packing: export carton marks, dimensions and weights. The report should arrive the same day with a pass or fail, key findings, photos and defect counts by severity. How to apply: before booking, send the inspector the PO, tech pack, approved sample, defect list, AQLs and level, packing and labelling instructions, and the list of tests you want. Hold the final balance until you have read the report and accepted it.

fails_when: Production is too early (under 80% packed) so the sample is not representative, or the product needs lab testing (chemicals, flammability) that an on-site inspection cannot do.

claim: Book a during-production inspection once about 20% of the order is produced, to catch defects while they can still be fixed and to get a predicted completion date.
body: A pre-shipment inspection can only tell you that 10,000 finished units are bad. A during-production inspection (DUPRO) at around 20% of output checks the first finished and semi-finished goods while most of the order is still raw material or on the line. QIMA's DUPRO covers production status (quantities of semi-finished, finished and packed goods, estimated capacity and predicted completion date), product specs (quantities, colours, style and construction, artwork, labels and tags, dimensions, product-specific tests) and packing (unit, inner and outer packs, export carton sizes, weights and shipping marks). Samples are drawn under ANSI/ASQ Z1.4 and the report comes the same day. How to apply: add a DUPRO for a first order with a new factory, a new product or material, a large order, or a launch date you cannot miss. Use the predicted completion date to warn your freight forwarder early if the vessel booking is at risk. Ask for corrective actions in writing after any finding, and keep the pre-shipment inspection as well.

claim: QIMA's 2026 data shows 8% of electronics and 11% of homewares orders from developed-market buyers fail AQL, versus 26% and 18% for emerging-market buyers with less mature QC.
body: This is a useful planning base rate: even buyers with mature quality programmes see roughly one inspection in 9 to 12 fail in these categories, and buyers with weaker programmes see one in 4 to 5. QIMA attributes the gap mainly to the buyer's quality control maturity (specs, defect lists, golden samples, consistent inspection) rather than to the factories themselves. How to apply: budget for failure. If you run 10 inspections a year in homewares, plan for about one failed lot, and price the follow-up: a re-inspection man-day (charge it to the supplier), rework time, and the delay to your launch or restock date. Build that delay into reorder timing rather than discovering it at the factory. Treat a failure rate well above these numbers as a sign your own specs and samples are the weak link, and fix them before switching factories. China still made up 35% of North America's QIMA service volume in Q2 2026, so most of this data reflects Chinese factories.

claim: Make every tech pack line traceable: a Pantone code for each BOM item, stitch type and stitches per inch, artwork distance from a seam, label positions, and a numbered revision log.

Bill of materials: fabric, secondary materials, trims and hardware, thread, labels and packaging, each with a colour name and Pantone code, never 'match body'. Example lines: 380 GSM shell, 160 GSM pocket lining, 1.4 yards of body fabric, 8 mm drawcord, 30 by 50 mm neck tag. Points of measure (body length from high point shoulder, chest width, sweep, sleeve length, neck drop) with grade rules per size (for example about 2 in chest circumference per size) and a tolerance for each. claim: Under Z1.4 switching rules, 2 rejected lots out of 5 in a row move a supplier to tightened inspection; 5 straight passes return it to normal; 10 straight passes allow reduced inspection.
body: AQL tables are built as a scheme, not a one-off test. The standard expects you to track each supplier's lots and switch plans. Normal to tightened: 2 of 5 consecutive lots rejected. Tightened to normal: 5 consecutive lots accepted. Normal to reduced: 10 consecutive lots accepted, steady production and your approval. Reduced back to normal: any lot rejected. If failures continue while on tightened, the standard tells you to stop accepting lots until the supplier fixes the process. Tightened keeps the same sample size but lowers the accept number (code letter L at AQL 2.5 drops from 10 to 8 majors). Reduced cuts the sample to about two fifths (letter L goes from 200 to 80 units), which cuts inspection days. How to apply: keep a simple log per factory and SKU family of each inspection result. Write the switching rule into the supplier agreement, with tightened inspections and re-inspections at the supplier's cost. Use reduced inspection as a reward you can offer a good factory instead of a price concession, since it shortens their inspection day and your bill. A common misuse of the standard is ignoring switching entirely, which lets a slipping supplier keep passing on luck.

claim: A letter of credit pays the seller only against documents that match its terms, so it protects the buyer too; a documentary collection is cheaper but banks do not check anything, so recourse is limited.
body: The US government's trade finance guidance ranks payment methods by who carries the risk. Cash in advance puts all of it on the buyer. Open account, usually 30, 60 or 90 days after shipment, puts it on the seller and is rare from Chinese factories for new buyers. A letter of credit sits between: your bank commits to pay once the seller presents documents that comply with the credit, so no money moves until the goods have shipped as described on paper. A documentary collection is a lighter option where banks only pass documents and collect payment, at sight or on a set date, but they do not verify the documents, so if something is wrong you have little recourse. How to apply it: for a first large order with a new factory, ask your bank for an L/C quote and list the documents you need, especially an independent inspection certificate. Remember the L/C checks paper, not goods, so the inspection certificate is what links payment to quality. Use a documentary collection only with a supplier you already trust.

claim: Default consumer-goods AQLs are 0 for critical, 2.5 for major and 4.0 for minor defects; one critical defect fails the lot and minors are cosmetic flaws on non-central zones.
body: Inspection firms classify each defect before counting it against the AQL. Critical means a breach of mandatory safety rules or a risk to health: a broken needle left in a garment, a failed hi-pot or earth-continuity test, sharp plastic or metal edges on a toy, hair, mould, blood or insect traces in any product or pack. Critical carries AQL 0, so a single one in the sample fails the shipment. Major means the product is likely to fail, be hard to use, or look bad enough to hurt sales: open seams and loop stitches on apparel, plush toys under or over stuffed, a power bank whose real capacity differs from its label. Major uses AQL 2.5 (in a 200-piece sample, accept 10, reject 11). Minor means outside the standard but not affecting use, mostly small spots, scratches, dust marks or slight shade shift on less visible zones (B and C areas). Minor uses AQL 4.0 (accept 14, reject 15 in 200). How to apply: write your own defect list per product with each defect assigned a class, and attach it to the PO and the inspection booking. Move anything that drives returns or reviews for your brand up a class: many brands treat a misplaced logo or printed claim as major because it damages the brand. Define zone A (front, visible in use) where even small flaws count as major.

fails_when: Premium or luxury goods where buyers expect tighter limits (AQL 1.0 for majors is common), or regulated goods where the law, not the AQL, sets the bar.

claim: The Pink Sheet updates monthly in the first few business days (4 May, 3 Nov and next 2 Dec in 2026), and the World Bank's price forecasts come twice a year, in April and October.
body: Knowing when each source posts lets you set a fixed monthly routine for cost watching. The World Bank's commodity markets page holds three free files: the Pink Sheet PDF, a monthly prices spreadsheet (history back decades) and an annual prices spreadsheet. The May 2026 edition is dated 4 May; the November edition posted on 3 November and the next is scheduled for 2 December, so each month's average lands within about the first two or three business days of the next month. The Commodity Markets Outlook adds price forecasts by commodity; the October 2026 edition is out and the next is due April 2027. Its October 2026 headline: commodity prices are set to rise 23% in 2026, with metals at record highs. How to apply it: on the first Monday after the Pink Sheet posts, pull the latest month for each series mapped to your BOM and update the cost model. Use the latest Outlook forecast for each commodity as your base case for the next year, and your own volatility band for the high and low cases. When the Outlook is six months old, check whether prices have already moved past its forecast before relying on it.

claim: Any Indian business selling hallmarked gold must register with BIS (free, online, valid for life); hallmarking falls on the first sale, pieces under 2 grams are exempt, and charges are itemised on invoices.
body: The Bureau of Indian Standards' page for jewellers says every manufacturer, wholesaler, distributor or retailer selling hallmarked gold or silver must register with BIS, which is done online through the NSWS portal, granted at once, free and valid for life. Mandatory hallmarking of gold jewellery and artefacts applies in the districts listed in the Mandatory Hallmarking Order as amended, and the duty sits with whoever makes the first point of sale, so an item is hallmarked once in the chain. The exemption list includes articles under 2 grams, kundan, polki and jadau jewellery, gold thread, gold watches and fountain pens, articles for export to a buyer's specification, items not yet complete, bullion forms, and jewellers with annual turnover up to Rs 40 lakh, who may register voluntarily. Hallmarking charges must be shown separately on the sales invoice; printing the HUID on invoices is voluntary. Under the BIS Act 2016 a breach can bring imprisonment and fines of at least Rs 1 lakh, rising to five times the value of the goods, and buyers of under-purity items are owed twice the shortfall plus testing charges. How to apply: register before launch, buy only HUID-marked stock from suppliers, and add a hallmarking line to invoices.
